title: Gypsophila: A Scalable and Bandwidth-Optimized Multi-Scalar Multiplication Architecture
problem: Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) is computationally intensive and bandwidth-constrained, particularly in Zero-knowledge proof systems. Scaling MSM to multiple processing elements results in high area overhead and bandwidth pressure.
motivation: MSM is a fundamental cryptographic primitive crucial for Zero-knowledge proof systems, requiring efficient hardware acceleration for practical deployment.
method: The paper optimizes individual MSM processing elements using bucket methods (grouping similar operations to reduce conflicts) combined with greedy scheduling (choosing the best next step at each point). To scale to multiple processing elements, the computation flows through three stages—bucket classification, bucket aggregation, and result aggregation—that balance the work. The key is sharing hardware: instead of each processing element having its own input channel and output handler, multiple elements share a single universal input channel and one post-processing unit. This sharing works because the processing elements have different data access patterns that don't interfere with each other, so one shared path can efficiently feed all of them while cutting both the hardware needed and the data traffic congestion.
key_novelty: Multiple MSM processing elements can operate efficiently in parallel by sharing a single universal input channel and post-processing unit, which eliminates redundant hardware and prevents bandwidth bottlenecks that would otherwise limit scaling.
contributions: Optimized single MSM PE achieving 2x average speedup (3.63x peak) over prior implementations
